rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God addresses the Prophet instead of his opponents; this indirect warning implies what awaits the disbelieving opposition.
rows.anchor: instead of addressing those who were opposing the Prophet (sws) and asking them to do something, God has directly addressed him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet should disregard disbelievers and hypocrites, ignore their mischief, and rely on God alone.
rows.anchor: The verse asks him to pay no heed to what these disbelievers and Hypocrites say, ignore their mischief and trust God alone.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word iṭāʿa here means paying heed and giving importance or regard.
rows.anchor: means to pay heed and give importance and regard. This is one of the common meanings of the word.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The harm refers to hypocrites’ excesses over Zaynab and earlier over ʿĀʾishah, with more discussed later in the sūra.
rows.anchor: refers to harms inflicted and excesses committed by the Hypocrites in the matter of Zaynab (rta) and earlier in the matter of ‘Ā’ishah (rta)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to leave them means to shun them in disgust at their conduct.
rows.anchor: signifies leaving them by showing disgust at their attitude.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s sufficiency reassures the Prophet and threatens his opponents; he should leave their case to God.
rows.anchor: The Prophet (sws) should leave their matter to God, Who is sufficient to deal with them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Before Muḥammad, prophets did not claim finality; each foretold the prophet who would follow.
rows.anchor: each prophet has prophesied about the next one after him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Adam allayed the angels’ fear about the khilāfah by naming the prophets.
rows.anchor: by enumerating the names of the prophets, Adam (sws) tried to allay the fears of the angels.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham prayed for prophets among both Isaac’s and Ishmael’s descendants, and the prayer’s acceptance is reported in scripture.
rows.anchor: regarding sending prophets in both branches of his descendents – the progeny of Isaac (sws) and the progeny of Ishmael (sws)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Israelite prophets foretold successors and sometimes introduced them to people through baptism.
rows.anchor: each prophet not only prophesied about the next one, but in many cases in accordance with the Israelite tradition even introduced him to people by baptism.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses also predicted Muḥammad as the seal of the prophets.
rows.anchor: He has also predicted about Muḥammad (sws), the seal of the prophets.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: John said his mission prepared the way for the prophet after him, Jesus; Jesus’s response convinced John his mission was fulfilled.
rows.anchor: John (sws) is one of the last prophets of the Israelites. He has stated that his mission was to clear the way for the prophet after him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He cites Jesus’s prediction in 61:6 that a messenger named Aḥmad would follow him.
rows.anchor: His name is Ahmad.” (61:6)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jesus’s Gospel predictions about Muḥammad were discussed earlier under al-Aʿrāf 7:157.
rows.anchor: The predictions of Jesus (sws) regarding Muḥammad (sws) in the Gospels have been cited in this tafsīr while explaining verse 157 of Sūrah al-A‘rāf.

rows.speaker: Imām Ḥamīd al-Dīn Farāhī
rows.claim: Farāhī interprets Jesus’s Gospel glad tidings of the Kingdom of Heaven and its parables as referring to Muḥammad’s prophethood and its attributes.
rows.anchor: In the opinion of my mentor, Imām Ḥamīd al-Dīn Farāhī, the glad tidings of the Kingdom of Heaven given by Jesus (sws) in the Gospels and the parables he has mentioned in this regard all relate to the prophethood of Muḥammad (sws)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prophets foretold successors until Muḥammad, whom God called the seal; he repeatedly declared that no prophet would follow, since a later prophet would have been foretold.
rows.anchor: on Muḥammad (sws) this practice completely ends. God has unequivocally called him the seal of the prophets

rows.speaker: The Prophet (sws)
rows.claim: The Prophet begins a parable comparing himself and earlier prophets to a beautiful building with a gap for one brick.
rows.anchor: I and the prophets before me can be likened to a person who constructed a beautiful building but in a corner there was a gap

rows.speaker: The Prophet (sws)
rows.claim: Completing the building parable, the Prophet says he is the missing brick and the seal of the prophets.
rows.anchor: So I am that brick and I am the seal of the prophets.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jesus likewise foretold Muḥammad, using the image of a rejected stone becoming the cornerstone.
rows.anchor: Jesus (sws) has also prophesied the arrival of Muḥammad (sws) in almost the same words.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Despite Jewish scholars’ efforts to conceal predictions, God conferred Muḥammad’s ordained role as the final prophet and messenger and last brick of the sharīʿah.
rows.anchor: In spite of all these efforts, the status the Almighty had ordained for Muḥammad (sws) was conferred on him at all cost.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Finality follows from religion’s completion, which is stated in 5:3.
rows.anchor: The finality of prophethood is also the essential consequence of the completion of religion mentioned in the verse

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If religion required no completion, prophets would remain continuously necessary; once religion was completed, prophethood necessarily ended.
rows.anchor: Had religion belonged to the category of things which never needed completion, then the prophets and messengers were indeed needed continuously.

rows.speaker: The Prophet (sws)
rows.claim: The Prophet states that messengerhood and prophethood ended after him and that neither a messenger nor prophet will come.
rows.anchor: The Prophet (sws) stated: “The [institutions of] messengerhood and prophethood have been terminated after me. Neither a messenger nor a prophet will now come.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet declared finality emphatically and also clarified whether any component of prophethood remained and what it would be.
rows.anchor: the emphasis with which the Prophet (sws) has declared the termination of his propethood, with the same stress he has also clarified whether after him any component

rows.speaker: The Prophet (sws)
rows.claim: In another report the Prophet’s final name, ʿĀqib, is explained as the one after whom no prophet comes.
rows.anchor: Similarly, in another narrative88 he has mentioned his various names. The last of these is عاقب and he himself has explained it as:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prophethood has only the one type described in Qurʾān and Ḥadīth, though prophet and messenger differ as explained elsewhere.
rows.anchor: nubuwwah (prophethood) is not of various types. It only has one type which is the one mentioned in the Qur’ān and Ḥadīth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects sectarian categories of prophethood as self-invented and absent from Qurʾān and Ḥadīth.
rows.anchor: This classification of prophethood is self-styled on their part. The Qur’ān and Ḥadīth do not mention them

rows.speaker: The Prophet (sws)
rows.claim: Anas reports that the Prophet reassured listeners that mubashshirāt remain as good Muslim dreams, a component of prophethood.
rows.anchor: The Prophet (sws) said: “Mubashsharāt do remain.” People asked: “God’s Messenger! What are the mubashsharāt?” He replied: “the dream of a Muslim

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mubashshirāt are glossed in other reports as nice or good dreams.
rows.anchor: Some narratives explain the meaning of ُاتَرِّشَبُم as ا الحسنةیؤُالر nice dream) and ا الصالحةیؤُالر good dream).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After Muḥammad, divine revelation ended; good dreams alone remain from prophethood, excluding claims to inspiration, divine experience, or visions.
rows.anchor: The only component left from the institution of prophethood is good dreams that a person sees.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Any Muslim may see a good dream; it confers no prophetic status or binding direction and is only good news or an omen.
rows.anchor: good dreams can be seen by any Muslim or true believer. They are not specific to anyone.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author calls claims of shadow or burūzī prophethood satanic, arguing the Prophet would have mentioned them if they remained.
rows.anchor: terms like ẓillī nubuwwah or burūzī nubuwwah (shadow prophethood) are totally satanic in nature.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Preservation of the Qurʾān follows necessarily from finality: earlier prophets could be followed by successors who restored changed teachings, but no successor follows Muḥammad.
rows.anchor: The arrangement made by God to protect the Qur’ān is a necessary consequence of termination of prophethood.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since the Qurʾān is preserved as the divine standard of good and evil, no later revelation or prophet is needed.
rows.anchor: The real divine barometer to judge good and evil is the Qur’ān. If it is preserved in its original form, no need remains of any divine revelation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ummah collectively bears witness to truth and reforms people, and scholars are accountable to God for this duty.
rows.anchor: As for the obligations of shahādah ‘alā al-nās (bearing witness to the truth before people) and reforming people, they rest with the ummah in its collective capacity.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hadiths predict that scholars and reformers will continue to arise in the ummah to address evils caused by mischief-makers.
rows.anchor: It has been mentioned in Aḥādīth that scholars and reformers will continue to be born in this ummah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: No prophet can appear before the Day of Judgement; when reports conflict with explicit revelation, reconcile them if possible, otherwise prefer Qurʾān and established religion.
rows.anchor: there is no possibility of any prophet appearing before the Day of Judgement. This inference is validated by the Qur’ān and Sunnah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage supplements the ordinary polygamy rule in 4:3: Muslims with more than four wives divorced the excess, while the Prophet had four until marrying Zaynab, so his doing likewise is unproven.
rows.anchor: These verses are basically a supplement to verse 3 of Sūrah al-Nisā’ in which the directive of polygamy is mentioned for common Muslims.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the Prophet married Zaynab, hypocrites objected that he had a separate sharīʿah; God explained his special permission regarding wives.
rows.anchor: Later, when he married Zaynab (rta), the Hypocrites objected to it by saying that he has his own sharī‘ah than the rest of his followers.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet may retain wives whose dowries he paid, without exception.
rows.anchor: The wives whose dowries have been paid by the Prophet (sws) are legally permissible to him without any exception.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He may marry slave-maidens received in battle after freeing them.
rows.anchor: If he wanted to marry slave-maidens received by him in a battle after liberating them, he could do so.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He may marry a close female relative who migrated with him for religion, leaving her own relatives.
rows.anchor: He could marry any woman among his close relatives who had migrated with him for the cause of religion after leaving their own relatives.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He may marry a believing woman who gifts herself to him.
rows.anchor: He could marry a believing woman who gifted herself to him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because these marriages served religion and the Muslim community, marital-right restrictions applying to ordinary Muslims were lifted for him.
rows.anchor: Since all these marriages were conducted to benefit religion and the Muslim community, the restrictions imposed regarding marital rights on common Muslim were lifted from him.
